97.1.before: Bring the challenge back gradually, and only when you want to and you're recovering well. Some people try to toughen themselves up in a cauldron, but what you're looking for is the edge where you can actually learn. And what about those hard dreams, or images that pop up during a session? They can show what feels important or frightening right now. Sometimes they show what feels missing, or what feels needed. They aren't evidence that what you saw in them happened, though, and shouldn't be used to confirm a memory or rebuild one. Or to suggest one.

97.2.start: When you catch it, look around
97.2.before: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" If nobody is in danger, take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

97.3.start: The opposite extreme of our pendulum
97.3.before: The opposite extreme of our pendulum, throwing everything transient away, as some people do with "thought-noting" practice, also isn't healthy, except as a meditation exercise. Transient feelings and thoughts can be meaningful signals. For example, if you don't want to be touched, say no now and work out what it means later. Same if something might be dangerous right now, or might be a medical warning sign: step away or get checked first.

97.5.start: Or if you do get an answer
97.5.before: Or if you do get an answer, it could come in different forms, like as a voice or just a hunch. It's often more like a feeling. Maybe grief or anger. If so just listen and be present for it if that's what it wants. If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you're calm and you've checked it against what you actually know (if you're in danger, get safe first).

97.7.before: Any of those reactions, from mania to paranoia, can also point to a vulnerability in you, so I'd be careful with other drugs that mess with what's real too, though I don't mean every drug's dangerous for you. And any predisposition toward mania or psychosis is a warning sign too, whether it's family history, a bad environment or a bad mindset. I can't tell you exactly what to do about it, and nobody can tell you for sure what's best for you. There are just caution signs, and when you see them, you take more precautions of every kind. You have to figure out what they mean for you, and if you can't, get help from trusted advisors.

Don't suddenly quit a prescribed medicine, or anything your body is dependent on, just because it might be part of the problem; have a doctor help you stop safely.

97.9.start: If a voice or urge is directing
97.9.before: If a voice or urge is directing you towards harm, and you feel at risk of acting on it, as with myself and those ghosts at home, move away from that open window and get some outside support. Know the limit of what you can handle, but don't turn it into a prison for life.

97.10.start: But if you're still thinking of staking
97.10.before: But if you're still thinking of staking your life on the opposite claim, that death is just nothing, look into that claim first (and if you're at the edge right now, the first step above comes before any of this). Researchers at the [University of Virginia](https://med.virginia.edu/perceptual-studies/2025/01/09/uvas-division-of-perceptual-studies-launches-major-research-initiative-on-childrens-past-life-memories/) have been collecting cases of small children who talk about a past life for about sixty years, and there's a big pile of near-death accounts too. I don't think any of it can tell you what dying will be like for you, but I'd read a few of those cases before betting my life on "nothing."

97.11.before: My father used to tell suicidal people, "Oh, you want to kill yourself? That's wonderful. Now you can change what you've always been too afraid to change in your life, and then see if you still want to end it!" His point wasn't that dying is wonderful. If everything's already on the table, what's the change you still can't bring yourself to make? Leaving? Quitting? Moving? Telling your family who you really are? Those aren't free, and you can't always take them back, but they're smaller than dying, and they can wait until you're calmer and have some help. Look at that life you've been afraid to change while you still have a human body.

97.13.before: Rumi says you have to keep breaking your heart until it stays open. Some people find that deep grieving gives way to warmth, or to feeling connected. Some feel held, in the body. Being loved can open grief, too. Someone takes care of you, and you think, "Why does this make me sad?" It can be sadness for the care that was missing. While you're present and still choosing, stay with it. Crying that deep can overwhelm you, too. It can retraumatize, mostly when nobody's with you or you've disappeared into the sadness. Once it's swamping you instead of opening you, slow down (like turning the song off for the night).

97.14.before: Then there are people you’re just getting to know. Meeting them can turn into a kind of test--”First impressions are everything,” as they say, but it could be even worse than that, if you need them to prove you’re lovable. Nobody’s a reassurance machine. I’m giving you permission now to quit school and flunk the tests. Get curious about who this person is, and who you are, and let both of you have your own reasons for being there in the beautiful present. Leaning on each other is still a big part of relationships, and it goes both ways. In a real crisis, getting a safe person involved can be exactly the right move.

98.2.start: After the day, look at what
98.2.before: After the day, look at what actually happened. If you did the Protector action(s), not feeling better right away is information to learn from. It doesn't mean failure. Healing is nonlinear, and sometimes standing up for yourself might make you feel worse at first. Not doing it is harder to figure out. Fear is the first guess, but maybe you didn't know how or why. Being worn out can stop you too, and sometimes whoever said they'd help couldn't make it. Hey, we've all been there. 🤗

98.5.before: Lucia Capacchione, an art therapist, wrote a whole book on this one, [The Power of Your Other Hand](https://www.luciac.com/). As titles go, it's pretty literal. Your other hand, the clumsy one, writes like a first grader anyway, so it gets the scared or hurt feelings (nothing made up). The usual hand answers, as the grown-up. Some people who get nothing but silence from their little one are surprised by what the other hand comes up with. A protective part might grab the pen first, and then it gets that hand until it's had its say.

98.6.start: Does saying it make the memory
98.6.before: Does saying it make the memory fiction? Well, no, it's still what happened, as far as you remember it, even if some details turn out fuzzy. And nobody's off the hook (you included, if you were the one who did the harm): whatever repair is owed is still owed. If the phrase does the trick, leave it at that, no need to narrate the whole thing.

98.7.before: Sometimes the session itself goes really well. You feel real care for your little one and say exactly what they needed to hear. And a few days later you're skipping lunch and saying yes to everything again. A lot of people's first guess is that they didn't go deep enough. I don't think that's it, though, and I don't think this one failed either. Maybe the grown-up just hasn't come out of the exercise with you yet. Whatever you did for your little one in there, I'd try a tiny bit of it out here, like texting a friend that you're having a rough day instead of saying you're fine. That can honestly be harder than the meditation was. One small thing like that can teach your little one more than ten more good meditations. It doesn't have to happen after every session.

98.11.start: Your little one can get really loud
98.11.before: Your little one can get really loud in the gap after one life ends and before the next one has formed. A breakup will do it, or moving to another country, an illness, losing your faith or a role, your youngest moving out. Maybe you've left a family or community, maybe you've stayed on new terms. A therapist or helper might step back because you're doing so much better, and suddenly your little one is wailing. For a while the old you is gone and the new you hasn't shown up yet. Tibetan Buddhism calls an in-between state like that a bardo (I'm only borrowing the word, so what it teaches about death and rebirth is up to you).
